A successful in-memory trial proves that its retained input passed the configured
checks. It does not reserve a future source version or promise that a later run
will see the same external data. Definition construction does not read or write
sources. Execution can do both.

Lake releases preserve published versions during ordinary publication. Publication
coordinates registry state and storage, but a process crash can leave intermediate
objects. Inspect interrupted runs and use the lake recovery and cleanup functions
before retrying. Do not assume an external target adapter provides the same
transaction or recovery guarantees as a managed lake.

Local lake writes require one coordinated writer. Do not run independent local
writers against the same catalog. Shared writers require the supported PostgreSQL
coordination configuration; using an object store alone does not provide locking.
The PostgreSQL integration job exercises separate writer processes. Backend and
crash behavior still require testing against the deployment configuration.

Writer bookkeeping is process-local and keyed to the connection configuration.
A future or targets worker must open its own resources and close those it owns.
Do not serialize live database connections into workers. Definitions are ordinary
R values; closures supplied by users can themselves capture mutable state.

“Immutable” describes normal release publication, not a legal retention policy or
undeletable storage. Operators must define retention for data, registry metadata,
quality evidence, frozen reports, backups and downstream catalogs. Deleting one
release does not erase its copies. Resolve deletion requests across those stores;
DataRaft does not provide a universal subject-erasure operation.

## What validation establishes

A declared contract checks its schema and configured constraints. Without a
contract, schema and type evidence is `unvalidated`, including reports and release
metadata. Non-empty checks and explicit quality rules can still run. Execution
status (`completed` or `published`) and validation status are separate facts.
Warnings permit publication by design and are not equivalent to passed checks.

Generic targets receive the in-memory snapshot that was checked. Lake execution
materializes candidates before checking and publication. These paths close the
check/write gap; arbitrary adapter writers remain responsible for writing the
provided snapshot without rereading the original source. Materialization and
integrity verification currently require memory proportional to the release.

Static inspection of random/time calls and repeated rule evaluation catch common
nondeterminism. They cannot prove arbitrary R code pure or detect every external
state change. Explicit dynamic references remain non-cacheable. Volatile checks
are labelled and excluded from cache reuse and frozen-report approvals. Neither
classification turns an external service into a reproducible input.

## Release integrity and maintenance

New releases record a SHA-256 digest of typed row content, independent of row
order and including duplicate rows. `dr_verify_releases()` checks content,
existence, originating runs and registry identity. Old releases without a recorded
baseline are `unverifiable`; migration does not retroactively certify them.
The digest is not a signature. A database administrator able to rewrite both data
and evidence can defeat it. Use access control and independently retained evidence
when that threat matters.

The local DuckDB registry enforces unique run and release identities with indexes.
DuckLake does not support those indexes: cooperating DataRaft writers check
uniqueness under catalog coordination, and verification detects duplicates. Direct
DBI writes bypass that protocol. Do not describe it as a database constraint on
DuckLake.

PostgreSQL-backed publication, ingestion, recovery, cleanup and snapshot expiration
share a catalog-level advisory lock. This intentionally serializes independent
assets as well as maintenance. Optimistic parent checks remain inside publication
transactions. Local deployments still require a single coordinated writer.
Failed publication attempts remove uncommitted candidate tables when the process
can run cleanup; a killed process requires `dr_interrupted()` and `dr_recover()`.
Cleanup recognizes quarantine candidates and preserves recorded releases.

## Adapter and IDE boundaries

Adapters must document atomicity, retries and partial failures for their backend.
`dr_test_adapter(failure_probe = ..., read_committed = ...)` can exercise a
specified injected failure and assert committed output is unchanged. A passing
probe does not establish every possible crash or backend failure mode.

The IDE bridge confines contract reads to the canonical `contract_root` supplied
by trusted R code, resolving symlinks and path components before containment
checks. Response writes have their own trusted root. These boundaries limit the
bridge protocol; they are not a sandbox for arbitrary code in the R session.
